title: Red Light Therapy for Exercise Recovery
subtitle: Evidence, protocols, and professional practice
audience: Fitness, wellness and recovery professionals (health clubs, recovery centres, boutique studios)
intro_notes: Welcome. In this course, you will learn what red light therapy is, what exercise recovery research reports, why protocols are hard to compare, and how to discuss this service honestly and within scope.

slides.title: What PBM is
bullets: PBM uses red or near-infrared light on body tissues [1, 2]
Lasers and LEDs differ in technical features [1]
Research protocols vary widely across settings [1, 2]
slides.notes: Photobiomodulation, or PBM, uses red or near-infrared light applied to the body [1, 2]. Reviews describe proposed effects on cellular metabolism, oxidative stress, and inflammatory signalling, but protocol differences make simple explanations difficult [1, 2]. Lasers and LED devices also differ technically [1].

slides.title: How it may work
bullets: Often described as support for bioenergetics [2]
Proposed pathways include oxidative stress signalling [2]
Human mechanism evidence is not settled [3]
slides.notes: PBM is often described as influencing bioenergetics and immune or oxidative stress pathways [2]. But one human study found a single PBM session did not increase mitochondrial respiration in skeletal muscle or skin tissue [3]. That means mechanism claims should stay cautious [3].

slides.title: Recovery and performance evidence
bullets: Sport recovery findings are promising but mixed [1, 4]
Some studies report better later recovery markers [4]
Primary short-term performance results may not differ [4]
slides.notes: A review reports promising effects for exertion recovery, including muscle strength, endurance, and reduced fatigue in sport performance studies [1]. In CrossFit athletes, PBMT-sMF did not beat other recovery methods for jump performance at one hour, but showed better jump results than passive recovery at 24 and 48 hours on secondary analysis [4].

slides.title: Pain and related outcomes
bullets: Some reviews report short-term pain benefits [6]
Other trials show no pain advantage over sham [8]
slides.notes: Evidence on pain is mixed across conditions [5, 6, 7, 8]. A fibromyalgia review reported consistent short-term pain and quality-of-life improvements, though heterogeneity limited generalizability [6]. In chronic trapezius myofascial pain, 808 nanometre laser was not superior to placebo for pain outcomes [8].

slides.title: Protocols and device choices
bullets: Key variables: wavelength, dose, timing, target [1, 2]
Examples range from 650 to 850 nm in studies [7, 9]
Not all published PBM methods suit fitness settings [10]
slides.notes: Protocol design matters because studies vary in wavelength, energy dose, timing, and application target [1, 2]. Examples in the brief include 650 nanometre LED use before exercise-induced muscle damage and 630 plus 850 nanometre LED use in low back pain research [7, 9]. Transcranial protocols are preliminary and not routine fitness-business practice [10].

slides.title: Safety, scope, and client talk
bullets: Adverse events were few in some trials [5, 7, 8]
Do not promise recovery, pain relief, or performance gains [1, 4, 8]
Keep disease and injury care outside fitness scope
slides.notes: Some included trials reported no adverse events or only mild and infrequent adverse effects, but safety reporting is not uniform across the literature [5, 7, 8]. Stay within scope. Present PBM as a wellness or recovery service, not a medical treatment. Be clear that evidence is promising in places, mixed in others, and not a guarantee [1, 4, 8].

takeaways: PBM research is promising, but results are mixed.
Protocol details drive outcomes and are not standardized.
Use cautious language and avoid medical claims.
Assess whether a published protocol fits your setting.
takeaways_notes: The main message is simple. PBM may support recovery in some contexts, but the evidence is not uniform. Your role is to understand the protocol, stay in scope, and communicate uncertainty clearly.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Red Light Therapy for Exercise Recovery
worksheet.instructions: Answer each prompt using only what was covered in the course. Keep your answers practical, cautious, and within fitness scope.

sections.heading: Section 1: Understanding the core ideas
prompts: In your own words, describe what photobiomodulation (PBM) is and what types of light it uses.
Summarize what the course said about how PBM may work, including why mechanism claims should be kept cautious.
Explain why the evidence for recovery and performance should be described as promising but mixed.

sections.heading: Section 2: Applying the content in practice
prompts: A gym member asks whether red light therapy will definitely improve their recovery after hard training. Write a short response that stays accurate to the course.
You are reviewing a published PBM protocol before offering a recovery service in a studio. What variables would you check, and why does fit-for-setting matter?
A coach wants to market PBM as a way to treat pain and boost performance for everyone. How would you reframe this service so it stays within scope and reflects the evidence?

sections.heading: Section 3: Safety, screening, contraindications, and referral
prompts: What did the course say about safety reporting and adverse events, and how should that affect the way you talk to clients?
Give two examples of client situations where you should avoid stepping outside fitness scope and refer them to an appropriate healthcare professional.
If a client asks you to use PBM as treatment for a disease or injury, how should you respond based on the course?
